Susan Saint James , the husky-voiced, Emmy-winning actress who starred in such popular TV series as McMillan & Wife, Kate & Allie and The Name of the Game , died October 26 of pancreatic cancer. She was 80.
A rep for Saint James confirmed her death to People. Among her survivors are husband Dick Ebersol, the former President of NBC Sports and executive producer of NBC’s Saturday Night Live.

In a statement, Saint James’ family described her as “generous with her time and energy, which she valued more than money, and instinctively drawn to whoever needed lifting up. She taught her children to pause, be kind and look out for other people.” Read the full statement below.
Born Susan Jane Miller on August 14, 1946, in Los Angeles, Saint James was raised in Rockford, Illinois, where she began modeling as a teen. She launched her acting career in a 1966 TV movie called Fame Is the Name of the Game, then booked guest roles in the series Ironside and, when the TV movie became a series titled The Name of the Game , Saint James landed a series-regular role. She won an Emmy for the role in 1969 and was nominated each of the two following years.
In 1968, she had a co-starring role in Where Angels Go, Trouble Follows , the sequel to popular comedy The Trouble with Angels.
Other TV episodic work from the era included roles in It Takes a Thief and Alias Smith and Jones, but her early signature role arrived in 1971 when she was cast opposite Rock Hudson in NBC’s light crime drama series McMillan & Wife , a highly popular program that had Saint James portraying the younger wife and partner in crime-solving. The show lasted for six seasons, with its finale on April 24, 1977, but Saint James had departed early over a contract dispute. Her character was killed off in a plane crash and the “& Wife” part of the title was erased. The show didn’t survive another season; by the end of her run, Saint James had received four Emmy nominations for her performance.
Saint James remained a prolific actor following her departure from the successful series, co-starring with Peter Fonda in the film Outlaw Blues (1977), George Hamilton in Love at First Bite (1979) and Jessica Lange and Jane Curtin in How to Beat the High Cost of Living (1980).
Saint James and Curtin would reunite four years later in what would become career high points for both stars. Their CBS sitcom Kate & Allie premiered on March 19, 1984, with the two stars portraying divorced mothers (and childhood friends) with children who decide to share a home in New York’s Greenwich Village. Saint James portrayed Kate, the more free-spirited of the two, with Curtin as the higher-strung conservative Allie. The combination proved a winner — and would be echoed decades later in the Jane Fonda-Lily Tomlin comedy Grace and Frankie — and the series, created by Sherry Coben, was a hit with critics and audiences, appreciated for its intelligent humor and warm, groundbreaking, chosen-family approach.
Saint James was nominated for two Emmys for her performance as Kate, with Curtin nominated for three and winning two.
In all, Saint James had eight Emmy noms — scoring one in five consecutive years from 1969-74 — including the win for her first.
Following Kate & Allie, Saint James largely retired from show business — she’d appear in guest roles periodically — devoting her time to raising a family that included two children from her second marriage, to make-up artist Thomas Lucas, and the three sons she had with third husband, the Saturday Night Live executive producer Ebersol. The couple met when she guest-hosted the NBC sketch comedy in 1981.
Tragedy struck on November 28, 2004, when a private plane carrying Ebersol and sons Charles and Teddy crashed at the Montrose Regional Airport in Colorado. Dick and Charles Ebersol survived, but 14-year-old Teddy was killed, along with a pilot and flight attendant. After her son’s death, Saint James often devoted her time working with parents who had lost children.
Saint James is survived by Ebersol, four children, seven grandchildren and sister Mary Mercedes Dewey.
“[Susan was] generous with her time and energy, which she valued more than money, and instinctively drawn to whoever needed lifting up. She taught her children to pause, be kind and look out for other people. “She never met a stranger. Every person she met became the most important person in the room at that moment, from a fellow board member to the clerk at the shoe store, who usually walked away knowing her entire life story. Her defining act: weeks after losing her youngest son, Teddy, in the November 28, 2004 plane crash, she delivered his eulogy as a note to each of her other children and her husband, giving them words to heal. Even in the deepest grief of her life, she put everyone else first. Days after the crash she sat with Tim Russert to thank the people who had reached out and to tell them the family was okay. “She brought that same fire and positivity to everything that followed, and never lost it. She is survived by her husband, Dick Ebersol, her four children–Sunshine Lucas, Harmony Lucas, Charlie Ebersol and Willie Ebersol–her seven grandchildren; her sister, Mary Mercedes Dewey, as well as her beloved service dog, Lola.”
